title: Shells, Ochre and Lines
subtitle: Symbols, ornaments and new technologies in Middle Stone Age Africa
summary: Long before the painted caves of Europe, people in Africa were collecting shellfish, heat-treating stone, making paint, drilling shell beads, engraving patterns, sleeping on insect-repellent bedding, hunting with arrows and burying a child. These innovations appeared piecemeal, and some came and went.
narration: About 100,000 years ago, in a cave above the Indian Ocean near the southern tip of Africa, someone ground red ochre to powder, mixed it with crushed bone, charcoal and fat, and stirred the paste inside two abalone shells. Archaeologists at Blombos Cave found the shells where they had been left, with the grinding stones beside them.

Blombos holds more. A flake of stone bears a crosshatched pattern drawn with an ochre crayon 73,000 years ago. Tiny snail shells, pierced and worn smooth by string, were once a necklace or a bracelet. Along the same coast at Pinnacle Point, people were gathering mussels 164,000 years ago and heating stone so that it would flake more cleanly. Further east, at Sibudu, they slept on beds of sedge topped with leaves that repel mosquitoes, glued stone tips to shafts and hunted with bows and arrows.
In Morocco, perforated shell beads are at least 142,000 years old. In Kenya, 78,000 years ago, a small child was laid in a grave with its knees drawn up and its head perhaps resting on a pillow.

For a long time archaeologists believed that art and ornament appeared suddenly in Europe, about 40,000 years ago. Africa tells a slower and more uneven story, in which new ideas flared, faded and returned over more than 100,000 years.

body.heading: Looking for the moment we became modern
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, the Upper Palaeolithic caves of Europe defined what archaeologists called “behavioural modernity”: art, ornaments, standardised bone tools and long-distance exchange, all appearing together around 40,000 years ago. Richard Klein proposed a genetic change in the brain about 50,000 years ago as the trigger. In 2000 Sally McBrearty and Alison Brooks published “The revolution that wasn’t”, arguing that in Africa these behaviours had appeared piecemeal across the Middle Stone Age, beginning more than 200,000 years ago. Discoveries since then have largely borne them out, while revealing a record that flickers on and off.

body.heading: Pinnacle Point: living from the sea
paragraphs: Pinnacle Point is a cluster of caves in the cliffs near Mossel Bay on South Africa’s south coast. In 2007 Curtis Marean’s team reported that people in cave PP13B were collecting brown mussels, limpets and other shellfish about 164,000 years ago, during a cold, dry glacial period, and grinding pieces of red ochre. The same levels contain small bladelets. Kyle Brown and colleagues showed in 2009 that the silcrete used for tools had been deliberately heated to make it flake more predictably, a process that requires controlled fire and hours of planning.

At the nearby rock shelter PP5-6, microliths (small blades blunted along one edge) appear about 71,000 years ago and continue for some 11,000 years (Brown and colleagues, 2012). Microliths are usually hafted in rows or as the tips of light projectiles, which implies composite weapons. Marean proposed a coastal adaptation hypothesis: predictable intertidal shellfish, harvested at low spring tides, allowed small populations to survive harsh glacial times on the southern coast and may have encouraged territorial cooperation.

Not every early innovation was coastal. At Ga-Mohana Hill in the Kalahari, hundreds of kilometres from the sea, Jayne Wilkins and colleagues (2021) found white calcite crystals and fragments of ostrich eggshell, apparently collected on purpose, about 105,000 years ago, when the region was wetter than today. Inland sites such as Border Cave and Sibudu, discussed below, add bedding, cooking, glues and arrows to the picture.

body.heading: Blombos Cave: paint, lines and beads
paragraphs: Blombos Cave, in a limestone cliff overlooking the Indian Ocean some 300 kilometres east of Cape Town, has been excavated by Christopher Henshilwood since 1991. In levels about 100,000 years old his team found two abalone shells used as containers for a red paste of ground ochre, crushed bone, charcoal and fat, with grinding stones beside them: a paint-making kit (2011).

Pieces of ochre from Blombos carry engraved crosshatched and parallel lines, the most elaborate about 75,000–77,000 years old. In 2018 the team reported a silcrete flake about 73,000 years old with a crosshatched pattern of nine red lines drawn with an ochre crayon, described as the oldest known drawing. Dozens of tiny Nassarius kraussianus snail shells, perforated and worn from being strung, some stained with ochre, date to about 75,000 years ago. The same Still Bay levels contain finely made bifacial spear points, some finished by pressure flaking, as well as bone awls and points.

At Diepkloof Rock Shelter on the west coast, Pierre-Jean Texier and colleagues (2010) reported 270 fragments of engraved ostrich eggshell, many from water containers, about 60,000 years old. The motifs, hatched bands and parallel lines, follow a limited set of rules that changed over time, which the authors read as a shared graphic tradition passed down the generations.

body.heading: Beds, glue and poisoned arrows
paragraphs: At Border Cave, on the border between South Africa and Eswatini, Lyn Wadley’s team found that by about 200,000 years ago people laid grass bedding, sometimes over layers of ash, which deter crawling insects (2020). The same cave preserved charred rhizomes of Hypoxis, a starchy plant, from about 170,000 years ago, evidence of cooking.

At Sibudu Cave in KwaZulu-Natal, bedding from about 77,000 years ago was built from sedges and rushes topped with leaves of the river wild-quince (Cryptocarya woodii), which contain chemicals that kill mosquitoes, and old bedding was periodically burnt (Wadley and colleagues, 2011). Sibudu’s toolmakers mixed plant gum with ochre to make compound glues for hafting stone tips, about 70,000–60,000 years ago, a recipe that requires adjusting ingredients and drying over a fire.

Sibudu also holds some of the earliest evidence for bows and arrows: quartz segments with impact fractures and residues from about 64,000 years ago (Marlize Lombard and Laurel Phillipson, 2010), and a bone point about 61,000 years old resembling arrowheads used by San hunters in recent times. A study published in 2026 reported traces of toxic alkaloids from Boophone disticha, a bulb used for arrow poison in southern Africa, on backed quartz tools about 60,000 years old from Umhlatuzana Rock Shelter, which would make them the oldest known poisoned arrows.

body.heading: Beads in North Africa
paragraphs: The oldest known shell beads come from Morocco. At Bizmoune Cave near Essaouira, El Mehdi Sehasseh, Steven Kuhn, Abdeljalil Bouzouggar and colleagues found 33 perforated shells of Tritia gibbosula, a small sea snail, in layers at least 142,000 years old (2021). At Grotte des Pigeons near Taforalt, similar beads, some coated with ochre, date to about 82,000 years ago. People carried such shells far inland, and they appear at several other Moroccan and Algerian sites, suggesting a long-lived tradition of personal ornament used, perhaps, to signal identity or alliances.

body.heading: A child laid to rest
paragraphs: In 2021 María Martinón-Torres, Nicole Boivin, Michael Petraglia and colleagues described the burial of a child of about two and a half to three years at Panga ya Saidi, a cave in the hills behind the Kenyan coast, dated by luminescence to about 78,000 years ago. The child, nicknamed Mtoto (“child” in Swahili), lay on its right side in a pit with the legs drawn up. The tightly flexed position suggests the body was wrapped, and the head may have rested on a perishable support. It is the oldest known deliberate burial in Africa. An infant from Border Cave, buried with a perforated cone shell, may be of similar age.

body.heading: Innovations that came and went
paragraphs: Middle Stone Age innovations did not accumulate in a straight line. Barbed bone points from Katanda on the Semliki River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, dated to about 90,000 years ago by several methods, look like harpoons of much later periods; some researchers doubt the dates because nothing similar appears again for tens of thousands of years.

In southern Africa, the Still Bay, with its bifacial points, and the Howiesons Poort, with its backed microliths and engraved eggshell, were dated by Zenobia Jacobs and colleagues (2008) to short windows around 72,000–71,000 and 65,000–60,000 years ago. Later work at Diepkloof and other sites suggests longer and more varied spans, but both industries still appear, flourish and vanish. Explanations include population size (larger, better-connected groups keep skills alive), climate change and shifting social networks.

debates.question: Was there a sudden “human revolution”?

views.label: A late revolution
views.text: Richard Klein argued that a neural change about 50,000 years ago unlocked fully modern behaviour, pointing to the burst of art, ornaments and new tools that followed the dispersal from Africa. Paul Mellars and others saw a real threshold around 60,000–40,000 years ago, whatever its cause.

views.label: Gradual accumulation
views.text: Sally McBrearty and Alison Brooks (2000), followed by Christopher Henshilwood, Francesco d’Errico and many others, argue that the components of modern behaviour appeared piecemeal in Africa over more than 150,000 years, and that the European Upper Palaeolithic reflects demography and preservation rather than a new kind of mind.

debates.status: The gradualist view now dominates. Few researchers still seek a single genetic switch, but many agree that the density of symbolic evidence rose sharply after about 50,000 years ago, and debate why.

debates.question: Why did the Still Bay and Howiesons Poort appear and disappear?

views.label: Population size
views.text: Adam Powell, Stephen Shennan and Mark Thomas (2009) modelled cultural transmission and argued that complex skills are maintained only when populations are dense and well connected; when groups shrink or fragment, techniques are lost.

views.label: Environment
views.text: Others link the industries to shifts in climate and resources recorded in marine and cave records, arguing that people changed toolkits to suit new hunting conditions.

views.label: Social networks and choice
views.text: Some researchers stress that the industries begin and end at different times at different sites, suggesting regional social networks and cultural choices rather than a single driver.

debates.status: The better dated the sites become, the less synchronous these industries look, which favours local and social explanations combined with demography. More precise dating at many sites is the key.

debates.question: Did coastal living make people modern?

views.label: Coastal adaptation
views.text: Curtis Marean argues that dense, predictable shellfish on the southern coast supported larger, more territorial groups, which favoured cooperation, planning and symbolic signalling, as seen at Pinnacle Point and Blombos.

views.label: Inland evidence too
views.text: Lyn Wadley and others point to bedding and cooking at Border Cave, glues and arrows at Sibudu, and crystals and ostrich eggshell collected about 105,000 years ago at Ga-Mohana Hill in the Kalahari, showing innovations far from the sea.

debates.status: The coast was clearly one important setting, but not the only one. Most researchers now see innovation spread across many environments, with the coast especially well preserved and well studied.

keyFacts.label: Oldest shell beads
keyFacts.value: Bizmoune Cave, Morocco, at least 142,000 years

keyFacts.label: Oldest burial in Africa
keyFacts.value: Mtoto, Panga ya Saidi, Kenya, about 78,000 years

keyFacts.label: Early arrows
keyFacts.value: Sibudu, about 64,000 years; poisoned tips reported from Umhlatuzana, about 60,000 years

sites.name: Pinnacle Point
sites.summary: Coastal caves near Mossel Bay with shellfish, ground ochre and heat-treated silcrete from about 164,000 years ago (PP13B) and microliths from about 71,000 years ago (PP5-6).

sites.name: Blombos Cave
sites.summary: A cave with a 100,000-year-old paint kit in abalone shells, engraved ochre, the 73,000-year-old crosshatched drawing, Nassarius shell beads and Still Bay points.

sites.name: Diepkloof Rock Shelter
sites.summary: A rock shelter with 270 fragments of engraved ostrich eggshell containers whose motifs follow a shared graphic tradition.

sites.name: Sibudu Cave
sites.summary: A rock shelter with insect-repellent bedding, compound adhesives of gum and ochre, and some of the earliest evidence for bow-and-arrow hunting.

sites.name: Umhlatuzana Rock Shelter
sites.summary: A rock shelter whose backed quartz microliths carry traces of plant poison according to a 2026 study, the oldest known evidence for poisoned arrows.

sites.name: Border Cave
sites.summary: A cave in the Lebombo Mountains with grass bedding from about 200,000 years ago, cooked starchy rhizomes from about 170,000 years ago and an infant burial with a shell.

sites.name: Bizmoune Cave
sites.summary: A cave near Essaouira with 33 perforated Tritia gibbosula shells, the oldest known shell beads.

sites.name: Grotte des Pigeons (Taforalt)
sites.summary: A cave in northeastern Morocco with perforated Nassarius shell beads, some coated with ochre.

sites.name: Panga ya Saidi
sites.summary: A cave where a child of about three, nicknamed Mtoto, was buried in a pit, flexed and probably wrapped: the oldest known burial in Africa.
